title: Web Development & Security — Midterm Mock Exam
description: The full midterm question bank: chapters 1 to 7, 105 multiple-choice questions.

questions.question: Which technology defines the structure of a web page?
questions.explanation: HTML defines a page's structure. CSS styles it, SMTP sends email, and SQL Server is a database.

questions.question: What does a client do in the client-server model?
questions.explanation: The client sends requests, and the server processes them and replies, so option A describes the server.

questions.question: Which type of website shows the same fixed content to every user?
questions.explanation: A static website serves the same fixed files to every visitor; a dynamic website builds pages for each request or user.

questions.question: What does elastic provisioning do?
options: Creates a new HTML heading tag
questions.explanation: Elastic provisioning adds or removes resources as demand rises and falls, the opposite of fixed capacity.

questions.question: Which developer works on both the front end and back end?
questions.explanation: A full-stack developer works on both the front end (the browser side) and the back end (the server and database).

questions.question: What is HTML?
questions.explanation: HTML is a markup language: it labels content with tags but has no logic such as loops or variables, so it is not a programming language.

questions.question: Which HTML element contains the displayed page content?
questions.explanation: <body> holds everything shown on the page; <head>, <meta>, and <title> hold information about the page.

questions.question: Which HTML tag represents the highest-level heading?
questions.explanation: <h1> is the top-level heading; <h2> is one level below it.

questions.question: Which attribute specifies the destination of a hyperlink?
questions.explanation: href sets where a link points; src sets the source file of elements such as images and scripts.

questions.question: Which image attribute provides alternative text?
questions.explanation: alt gives text that is shown when the image cannot load and that screen readers read aloud; src is the image's file path.

questions.question: Which HTML element represents a block of navigation links?
questions.explanation: <nav> marks a block of navigation links; <header> is the introductory area of a page or section.

questions.question: Which HTML tag creates a table row?
questions.explanation: <tr> creates a table row; <td> creates a cell inside a row.

questions.question: Which form attribute specifies where submitted data is sent?
questions.explanation: action is the URL that receives the form data; method sets how it is sent (GET or POST).

questions.question: Which control allows one choice from a group sharing the same name?
questions.explanation: Radio buttons that share a name allow only one choice; checkboxes allow several.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute makes an input mandatory before submission?
questions.explanation: required stops the form from submitting until the field has a value; pattern checks the format of a value.

questions.question: What does CSS do?
options: It creates the structure of a web page.
It controls the style and layout of a web page.
It adds calculations to a web page.
It stores information about a web page.
questions.explanation: CSS controls style and layout. HTML creates the structure, which is what option A describes.

questions.question: Where is Inline CSS written?
options: Inside the HTML element using the style attribute.
questions.explanation: Inline CSS goes in an element's style attribute; CSS in a <style> tag inside the <head> is internal CSS.

questions.question: Which CSS type uses a separate .css file?
questions.explanation: External CSS lives in a separate .css file linked from the page; internal CSS sits in a <style> tag.

questions.question: Which symbol is used for a class selector in CSS?
questions.explanation: A class selector starts with a dot, as in .note; # is used for ID selectors.

questions.question: Which symbol is used for an ID selector?
questions.explanation: An ID selector starts with #, as in #menu; the dot is used for classes.

questions.question: What does the universal selector * select?
options: Only the element with a specific ID
questions.explanation: The universal selector * matches every element on the page.

questions.question: What is JavaScript mainly used for on web pages?
options: Defining the page's colors and fonts
Adding interactive features to web pages
Linking HTML to a CSS file
questions.explanation: JavaScript adds interactive behavior. Colors and fonts are CSS, and structure is HTML.

questions.question: Which command displays an alert dialog without a text input field?
questions.explanation: alert() shows a message with only an OK button; prompt() also shows a text input field.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to write JavaScript code?
questions.explanation: JavaScript goes inside <script> tags; <style> holds CSS.

questions.question: What does the DOM allow JavaScript to do?
options: Connect the computer to the internet
questions.explanation: The DOM represents the page as objects, so JavaScript can read and change its elements.

questions.question: Which event handler runs when a user clicks an element?
questions.explanation: onclick runs when an element is clicked; onmouseover runs when the pointer moves over it.

questions.question: What does innerHTML do?
options: Selects an element by its ID
Sets or returns an element's HTML content
questions.explanation: innerHTML gets or sets the HTML inside an element. Selecting an element by its ID is what getElementById() does.

questions.question: What is a variable used for in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: A variable stores a value under a name so the program can use it later.

questions.question: Which operator means "greater than"?
questions.explanation: > means greater than; >= means greater than or equal to.

questions.question: What is a function in JavaScript?
options: A CSS rule that changes colors
A block of code designed to perform a specific task
An HTML element used to display images
A variable that stores only text
questions.explanation: A function is a named block of code that performs a specific task when it is called.

questions.question: What does HTTPS help protect?
options: Data sent between the browser and server
questions.explanation: HTTPS encrypts data traveling between the browser and the server, so others on the network cannot read or change it.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is commonly used to retrieve data?
questions.explanation: GET requests data from the server; POST sends data to it.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a URL?
options: To identify the location of a resource on the web
questions.explanation: A URL is the address of a resource on the web.

questions.question: What does DNS do?
options: Translates domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS translates a domain name such as example.com into the IP address of its server.

questions.question: What can happen during DNS spoofing?
options: A website loads faster than usual
A user may be directed to a fake website
A server stores more website data
questions.explanation: In DNS spoofing, forged DNS answers can send the user to an attacker's fake website.

questions.question: Which technique can help protect against DNS spoofing?
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs DNS records, so resolvers can detect forged answers.

questions.question: What is SQL injection?
options: Injecting malicious SQL input to attack a database
Stealing a user's session cookie through a browser extension
Sending a user to a fake website using DNS spoofing
Tricking a user into making an unwanted request
questions.explanation: SQL injection puts malicious SQL into user input so that it runs against the database. Option D describes CSRF.

questions.question: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
options: A method for encrypting website traffic
A technique for managing user sessions
A method for checking user permissions
An attack involving malicious scripts running in a user's browser
questions.explanation: In XSS, a site delivers an attacker's script, which then runs in the victim's browser.

questions.question: Why should web applications validate user input?
options: To make web pages load without images
To help prevent malicious input and attacks
To allow every user to access all pages
To avoid using a web server
questions.explanation: Validating input rejects malicious or malformed data before it can be used in an attack.

questions.question: What is authentication?
options: Deciding which files a user can download
Tracking a user's activity across requests
questions.explanation: Authentication checks who the user is; deciding what they may access is authorization.

questions.question: What does access control determine?
options: What a user is allowed to access
How a domain name is translated
questions.explanation: Access control decides what a user is allowed to see or do.

questions.question: What is the purpose of session management?
options: To translate domain names into IP addresses
To encrypt every image on a website
To maintain a user's login state across requests
questions.explanation: Session management keeps a user logged in across separate HTTP requests, because HTTP itself does not remember them.

questions.question: What does a web server do?
options: Converts domain names into IP addresses
Receives requests and serves web content
Verifies a user's identity in every application
Prevents every type of cyberattack automatically
questions.explanation: A web server receives HTTP requests and sends back pages and other content.

questions.question: How does browser caching help?
options: It replaces the need for HTTPS
It can reduce loading time by reusing stored resources
It prevents users from submitting forms
questions.explanation: Caching keeps copies of resources, so the browser can reuse them instead of downloading them again.

questions.question: Where should important input validation and security checks be enforced?
options: Only in the browser's address bar
Only in the website's HTML design
questions.explanation: Users can change anything in their own browser, so the checks that matter must be enforced on the server.

questions.question: Where do client-side controls run?
questions.explanation: Client-side controls run in the user's browser, where the user can change them.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of client-side validation?
questions.explanation: Client-side validation gives the user quick feedback. It cannot protect the server, because it can be bypassed.

questions.question: Which side should enforce important security rules?
questions.explanation: Only the server is under the site's control, so it must enforce the security rules.

questions.question: Why can client-side controls be bypassed?
options: Users can modify browser code and values
questions.explanation: The browser is under the user's control: they can edit HTML, JavaScript, and request values with developer tools or a proxy.

questions.question: What can a user modify in the browser?
questions.explanation: A user can change HTML attributes and JavaScript in their own browser, but not the server directly.

questions.question: What should the server do with an invalid request?
options: Validate it and reject it if necessary
questions.explanation: The server must check every request and reject it if it is invalid.

questions.question: What is an advantage of client-side validation?
questions.explanation: Client-side validation gives fast feedback without a round trip to the server, but it provides no security.

questions.question: Why must the server validate user input?
questions.explanation: Server-side validation enforces the security rules, because client-side checks can be skipped.

questions.question: What is the best validation practice?
options: Validate on the client and server
Allow the browser to decide everything
questions.explanation: Validate in both places: on the client for fast feedback, and on the server for security.

questions.question: Why should a server not trust hidden fields?
options: They cannot be sent in HTTP requests
questions.explanation: A hidden field is only hidden from view; the user can still change its value before sending the form.

questions.question: What does disabling a button do?
options: Prevents the server from receiving requests
Guarantees that the action is protected
Restricts interaction through the normal interface
questions.explanation: A disabled button only blocks the normal interface; the user can still send the same request another way.

questions.question: How should an online store handle product prices?
options: Calculate or retrieve prices using trusted server-side data
Trust the price submitted by the browser
Use a hidden field as the final price
Rely only on JavaScript to calculate the price
questions.explanation: The server should look up or calculate the price from trusted data, because any price the browser sends can be changed.

questions.question: What does authorization determine?
options: Whether the user entered a password
Whether the user has permission to perform an action
questions.explanation: Authorization decides whether a user may perform an action; checking a password is authentication.

questions.question: Why is hiding an Admin button not enough?
options: Admin buttons must always be visible
The user may still access the endpoint directly
The browser cannot display admin pages
Hidden buttons automatically disable the server
questions.explanation: Hiding the button does not protect the admin endpoint, which the user can still request directly. The server must check permissions on every request.

questions.question: What should security testing check?
options: Whether the website has a good design
Whether the server rejects unauthorized or invalid requests
Whether the browser loads images quickly
questions.explanation: Security testing checks that the server rejects unauthorized or invalid requests, even when they are sent directly.

questions.question: Where is PHP code executed?
questions.explanation: PHP runs on the server, and the browser receives only its output.

questions.question: What is the usual file extension for PHP files?
questions.explanation: PHP files usually end in .php.

questions.question: Which opening tag starts a PHP code block?
questions.explanation: <?php starts a block of PHP code.

questions.question: Which symbol starts a PHP variable name?
questions.explanation: PHP variable names start with $, as in $name.

questions.question: Which function defines a constant in PHP?
questions.explanation: define() creates a constant; isset() checks whether a variable is set.

questions.question: Which PHP statement outputs text?
questions.explanation: echo outputs text; return sends a value back from a function.

questions.question: Which operator joins strings in PHP?
questions.explanation: PHP joins strings with the dot operator, as in "a" . "b"; + is for adding numbers.

questions.question: Which include statement stops execution if the file is missing?
questions.explanation: require stops the script with a fatal error if the file is missing; include only gives a warning and continues.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a function in PHP?
questions.explanation: The function keyword declares a function; class declares a class.

questions.question: What is a PHP array?
questions.explanation: A PHP array is an ordered map from keys to values, and the keys can be numbers or strings.

questions.question: What does $this refer to in a PHP method?
questions.explanation: $this refers to the object the method was called on, not to the class itself.

questions.question: Which superglobal contains query-string data?
questions.explanation: $_GET holds the query-string parameters from the URL.

questions.question: Which superglobal contains submitted POST form data?
questions.explanation: $_POST holds data sent with the POST method, usually from a form.

questions.question: Where must security validation of user input be enforced?
questions.explanation: Validation must be enforced on the server, because checks in the browser can be bypassed.

questions.question: When must header() be called relative to sending output to the browser?
questions.explanation: header() must be called before any output, because HTTP headers are sent before the page body.

questions.question: What does a DBMS do?
questions.explanation: A DBMS stores, retrieves, and manages the data in a database.

questions.question: What does a row represent in a relational table?
questions.explanation: A row is one record; a column is one attribute.

questions.question: Which key uniquely identifies each row in a table?
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key points to a row in another table.

questions.question: What is the role of a foreign key?
questions.explanation: A foreign key links a row to a related row in another table, usually by that table's primary key.

questions.question: Which data type is suitable for exact monetary values?
questions.explanation: DECIMAL stores exact values; FLOAT is approximate and can cause rounding errors with money.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of normalization?
options: Create a second copy of data
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes tables to reduce duplicated data and the update problems it causes.

questions.question: Which SQL command retrieves records?
questions.explanation: SELECT retrieves rows; INSERT adds them.

questions.question: Which SQL command adds a new record?
questions.explanation: INSERT adds a new row; UPDATE changes existing rows.

questions.question: Which SQL clause filters individual rows?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.question: Which SQL operation pairs rows from tables using a matching condition?
questions.explanation: JOIN combines rows from tables where a condition matches; UNION stacks the results of two queries.

questions.question: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation; WHERE filters rows before grouping.

questions.question: Which command undoes uncommitted transaction changes?
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK undoes changes that have not been committed; COMMIT makes them permanent.

questions.question: Which constraint prevents a required value from being NULL?
questions.explanation: NOT NULL requires a value in the column; UNIQUE forbids duplicate values but does not by itself require a value.

questions.question: Which technique most directly prevents SQL injection?
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries keep data separate from the SQL code, so input cannot change the query. Input filtering alone can be bypassed.

questions.question: What does least privilege mean for a database account?
questions.explanation: Least privilege gives an account only the permissions it needs, which limits the damage if it is compromised.

questions.question: What does authentication verify?
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who the user is; permissions are checked by authorization.

questions.question: Which control slows repeated password guesses?
questions.explanation: Rate limiting slows or blocks repeated login attempts, which makes password guessing slow.

questions.question: What is username enumeration?
questions.explanation: Username enumeration means finding out which usernames exist, often from different error messages or responses.

questions.question: Which login error helps reduce username enumeration?
questions.explanation: A generic "Invalid credentials" message does not reveal whether the username exists, while "Username does not exist" does.

questions.question: Which token is suitable for password recovery?
questions.explanation: A recovery token must be random and single-use, so it cannot be guessed or reused. A sequential token can be predicted.

questions.question: How should passwords be stored?
options: Image filenames in a public folder
questions.explanation: Passwords should be hashed with a unique salt and a slow algorithm, which makes cracking them much harder. Fast, unsalted hashes are easy to crack.

questions.question: What does fail-closed login behavior mean?
questions.explanation: Fail-closed means denying access when an error happens, instead of letting the user in.

questions.question: Why do web applications use session tokens?
options: To verify passwords on every request
To choose the monitor refresh rate
To change the physical keyboard layout
questions.explanation: A session token lets the server recognize a logged-in user on later requests without asking for the password again.

questions.question: Which source should generate secure session tokens?
questions.explanation: Session tokens must come from a cryptographically secure random source so they cannot be predicted; timestamp-based values can be guessed.

questions.question: Which cookie flag prevents JavaScript from reading a cookie?
questions.explanation: HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie; Secure only makes the browser send it over HTTPS.

questions.question: Which action helps prevent session fixation?
options: Keep the same token after login
questions.explanation: Issuing a new session token at login makes a token an attacker planted before login useless.

questions.question: What should happen to a session on logout?
options: Only redirect to the home page
Save the page as a desktop image
questions.explanation: Logout must invalidate the session on the server; a redirect alone leaves the old token usable.

questions.question: Which control helps protect state-changing requests from CSRF?
questions.explanation: An anti-CSRF token is a secret value the attacker's site cannot know, so forged requests are rejected. The browser sends the session cookie automatically, so the cookie alone does not help.

questions.question: What is vertical privilege escalation?
options: A user reads another peer account
A normal user gains admin access
A browser changes its default font
A server compresses an image file
questions.explanation: Vertical escalation means gaining a higher role, such as a normal user getting admin access. Reading a peer's account is horizontal escalation.

questions.question: Which check most directly prevents IDOR?
questions.explanation: IDOR is prevented by checking, for every object requested, that this user may access it. Authentication alone does not check ownership.
